title: The family table
hookLine: meals shared are a small communion
tomorrow: at night, what's the one question worth asking about your day?

cards: Phones in a basket by the door. Somebody spills the water again. A teenager answers in single words until, halfway through the pasta, he starts talking and doesn't stop.
Nothing about the scene looks holy. No candles, no incense. And yet the question under it is an old one: why would God care who you eat dinner with?

teach.b: The Catholic answer starts at the end of Luke. Two disciples walk to a village called Emmaus with a stranger who opens the Scriptures to them the whole way, and still they don't know him.
It's getting late, so they press him to stay. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "he took bread, and blessed, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him." Not on the road.
At the table. Acts says the first believers kept at it, "breaking bread from house to house, they took their meat with gladness and simplicity of heart."
The Catechism calls the Christian family a domestic church, a small church at home. Catholic teaching keeps one line clear: the Eucharist at Mass is a sacrament, and no dinner is that.
A meal faced together can echo it, which is why the line is a small communion, not the Communion. A neighbor tradition says something close.
In a hadith collected by Abu Dawud, some companions told the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that they ate and were never satisfied.
He asked if they ate separately, and told them to gather for their food and say God's name over it, and it would be blessed for them.
The name said over food is bismillah, in the name of God.
So both hear a blessing in eating together.

The honest difference: for Catholics the shared table points toward the Mass and the bread broken at Emmaus; in Islam there is no sacrament of bread, and the blessing is God's name spoken over an ordinary meal.

how: Many Catholic families say grace and eat together when they can, and the Church speaks of the family as a domestic church; Sunday dinner after Mass is a custom in many homes.

games.why: at Emmaus the stranger was known at the table, and the hadith says gather for your food. both put the blessing in the gathering.

practice: Make a small plan for your next meal with anyone, even if it's only you. Decide where the phone will go before the food arrives, and see the faces, or the plate, you'll be looking at instead.

wordCard.voice: The family table. A meal with people actually present, an echo of the bread broken at Emmaus.

orig.note: Greek: sharing, communion, fellowship; the word in Acts 2:42 for the first believers' common life.

carryVoice: Carry this: a small communion, bread passed and faces up. Enjoy the next meal together.
